temp: The average temperature across Earth's surface, including land and oceans. A lasting rise means the whole planet is getting warmer, even though individual places still have cold days. This warming changes rainfall and makes many heat extremes more likely.
methane: Releases of a gas that traps heat in the air. It can escape from oil and gas equipment or be produced by livestock, rice fields and rotting waste. The amount released each year is different from the amount already built up in the atmosphere.
deforestation: Clearing forests so the land can be used for something else, such as farming, roads or buildings. Removing trees takes away wildlife habitat and reduces the forest's ability to store carbon. Burning or rotting trees can also release carbon dioxide into the air.
industry_farming: Large-scale production of crops and livestock using machinery, fertilizers, feed and water. These systems supply food, but their effects depend on how they are managed. Heavy resource use can damage soil, pollute water and release gases that warm the planet.
food: How much crop and livestock production people need for food and other uses. Growing demand can require more land, water, feed and fertilizer. The amount produced does not tell us whether everyone has enough nutritious food or can afford it.
urbanization: The growth of towns and cities as more people live and work in them. Replacing plants and soil with buildings and roads can trap heat and leave rainwater with fewer places to soak into the ground. Planning and public services affect how these changes are managed.
fast_fashion: Making and selling large amounts of inexpensive clothing that is quickly replaced. Producing the fabric, dyeing it and transporting garments uses water and energy. Clothes that are discarded early also add to waste and pollution.
migration: People moving from one place to another to live. Heat, floods, drought and the loss of work can contribute to a decision to move, alongside many other causes. The effects depend on whether people can find safe housing, services and a reliable income.
resource_depletion: Using natural supplies faster than they can recover or be replaced. Examples include pumping underground water faster than rain refills it, or wearing away soil faster than new soil forms. This leaves less available for people and nature in the future.
carbon_emission: Carbon dioxide entering the air when fuels are burned, materials are made or forests are cleared. This gas builds up and holds in heat, contributing to long-term warming. The amount released is different from its concentration already in the air.
personal_conveyance: The vehicles people use for their own journeys, such as cars and motorcycles. Burning petrol or diesel releases gases that warm the planet and pollution that affects air quality. The impact depends on the vehicle, its energy source and how far and often it travels.
environ_anomalies: Two or more dangerous conditions happening together or close enough in time to make each other worse. For example, a drought can leave little water available when a heatwave arrives. The combined effects can be harder to manage than either event alone.
el_nino: A recurring climate pattern in which the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become unusually warm. The change shifts winds and rainfall far beyond the ocean itself. Some regions become wetter while others become drier. The effects vary between events.
la_nina: A recurring climate pattern in which the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become unusually cool. It changes winds and rainfall across many regions. The effects differ by place and season, so it does not mean that everywhere becomes colder or wetter.
amoc: A weakening of the large Atlantic Ocean circulation that carries warm water north near the surface and colder water south at depth. This movement helps distribute heat. A lasting change can affect rainfall, sea levels and marine life. One low reading does not establish a lasting slowdown.
wet_bulb_heat: Hot conditions made more dangerous by moist air. When the air is very humid, sweat evaporates less easily, so the body has more difficulty cooling itself. How dangerous the conditions become also depends on how long they last, activity and access to cooling.
monsoon_volatility: Changes in the timing, strength or reliability of a region's rainy season. Rain may arrive late, fall in intense bursts or stop for unusually long periods. These shifts can disrupt planting and water supplies even when the total seasonal rainfall looks normal.
permafrost_thaw: Ground that has stayed frozen for at least two years begins to soften as it warms. The surface can sink, damaging roads and buildings. Previously frozen plant material can also decay and release gases that add to warming.
rain_on_snow_flood_risk: The chance of flooding when rain falls onto existing snow. Rain and melting snow can send a large amount of water downhill in a short time. The outcome depends on the snow, the ground and how much water rivers and drains can carry.
peak_glacier_runoff_passage: The point after which a shrinking glacier supplies less meltwater over the long term. At first, faster melting may increase the water reaching rivers. Eventually, too little ice remains to keep that supply up, making water less reliable downstream.
marine_pathogen_range_expansion: Disease-causing germs in seawater becoming active in more places or for a longer part of the year. Warmer water can help some of these germs survive and multiply. This can affect seafood safety, marine animals and people who use coastal waters.
thermal_stratification_intensification: Water forming more strongly separated layers, often with warmer, lighter water above colder, denser water. The layers mix less easily. This can reduce the movement of oxygen and nutrients between the surface and deeper water.
delta_salt_intrusion_fronts: The inland edge of salty seawater moving through places where rivers meet the sea. Higher sea levels or weaker river flows can let salt travel farther upstream. Water used for farming or drinking can then become too salty.
oceanic_upwelling_disruptions: Changes in the process that brings deeper, nutrient-rich seawater toward the surface. Winds and ocean currents help drive this movement. If its timing or strength changes, the tiny organisms at the base of marine food chains may receive fewer nutrients.
extreme_precipitation_intensity: How heavily rain or snow falls during unusually strong events. A large amount arriving in a short time can overwhelm drains and rivers. The resulting flood risk also depends on the landscape, soil and buildings in the path of the water.
tropical_cyclone_rapid_intensification: A tropical storm's winds becoming much stronger in a short time. Warm seawater and suitable air conditions can help this happen. Fast strengthening can leave communities less time to prepare, particularly when a storm is approaching land.
pyrocumulonimbus_smoke_injection: A very intense wildfire creating a towering storm cloud that carries smoke high into the atmosphere. Smoke reaching these heights can travel far and remain in the air longer. These fire-driven storms behave differently from ordinary low-level smoke plumes.
coastal_permafrost_erosion: Waves wearing away shorelines whose ground was held together by ice. As the ground thaws and sea ice provides less protection from waves, the coast can break down faster. Nearby homes, roads and other structures can lose the land beneath them.
water_stress: How strongly people's water use competes with the available supply. When farms, households and businesses use a large share of that supply, there is less room to cope with dry periods. The needs of rivers and other living systems also matter.
groundwater_depletion: A lasting reduction in water stored beneath the ground. This happens when water is removed faster than it is replaced by rain and other flows. Wells can become less reliable, and rivers or wetlands fed by this water can also be affected.
heat_related_mortality_burden: Deaths linked to exposure to high temperatures. The risk depends on more than the temperature: age, health, housing, length of exposure and access to cooling all matter. Estimates need to distinguish deaths caused or contributed to by heat from deaths occurring for other reasons.
air_pollution_health_burden: Illness and deaths linked to breathing harmful particles or gases. Pollution can damage the lungs and heart, with effects depending on what people breathe and for how long. These health effects are not all caused by climate change.
occupational_heat_exposure: People facing hot conditions while doing their jobs, outdoors or inside warm workplaces. Physical effort can make it harder for the body to cool down. The danger depends on humidity, time spent working, protective clothing and access to rest and cooling.
data_centers: Buildings filled with computers that store information and run online services. The computers need electricity, and their heat must be removed. Their environmental effects depend on the power supply, cooling system, water use and location.
ai_data_centers: Computing facilities used to train or run artificial intelligence systems. Powerful processors can use large amounts of electricity and produce heat that needs to be removed. The resulting water use and pollution depend on the equipment, cooling method and energy supply.
semiconductor_fabs: Factories that make the tiny chips used in phones, computers and many other devices. Making these chips needs very clean water, power and carefully handled chemicals. It also creates waste and releases gases. The effects on nearby land, water and air depend on how the factory is run.
telecom_backbone: The main cables and equipment that carry phone and internet traffic between cities and countries. Many local connections depend on this network. Keeping it running requires electricity and reliable physical routes, which can be disrupted by damage or extreme conditions.
mobile_wireless_networks: Antennas and equipment that connect mobile devices without a cable to each user. The equipment still needs electricity and links to the wider communications network. Power cuts, heat or damaged connections can interrupt service.
internet_exchange_points: Places where separate computer networks connect and pass online traffic to one another. These hubs help information reach its destination. Damage or a power failure at an important hub can affect many services at once.
subsea_cables: Long communication lines laid on the seabed to carry information between places. They connect to land at coastal stations. If a busy route or landing station is damaged, internet and other communications can be disrupted.
food_waste: Food being lost or thrown away instead of being eaten. The land, water and energy used to produce it are then spent without providing a meal. Food rotting without much oxygen, such as in landfill, can also release a powerful heat-trapping gas.
aviation: Travel and freight carried by aircraft. Burning jet fuel releases carbon dioxide, while other emissions and the clouds aircraft can leave behind also affect the climate. Airports add their own needs for land, electricity and transport connections.
shipping: Moving people or goods by water. Vessels need energy, often from burning fuel, and depend on ports and usable routes. Their effects include air pollution, gases that warm the planet and pressure on marine environments.
cement_concrete: Materials widely used to build roads, bridges and buildings. Making the powder that binds concrete requires high heat and releases carbon dioxide when limestone is processed. Fuel use, quarrying and the amount of material needed all affect the total impact.
steel: An iron-based material used in buildings, vehicles and machinery. Producing it can require mining, very high temperatures and large amounts of energy. Its climate impact depends on the production method, energy source and use of recycled metal.
plastics_petrochemicals: Materials and chemicals commonly made from oil and gas, including packaging, fabrics and solvents. Making them uses energy and raw materials. Pollution can arise during production, use and disposal, including when waste reaches rivers or the sea.
air_conditioning_refrigerants: Equipment that moves heat out of rooms using electricity and circulating cooling gases. Some of those gases strongly warm the planet if they leak into the air. The total climate effect depends on the gas, leak prevention and electricity source.
fertilizer_production: Making substances that supply nutrients to crops. Manufacturing nitrogen-based products often uses fossil gas and large amounts of energy. Production and later use can release pollution, so factory emissions and effects on farms need to be assessed separately.
mining_critical_minerals: Extracting raw materials used in batteries, electrical networks and electronics. Mining can disturb land, use water and energy, and leave waste that needs careful management. Its effects depend on the material, location and safeguards at the site.
urban_sprawl_housing: Homes and roads spreading outward over larger areas, often with buildings far apart. This can replace farmland or wildlife habitat and make longer car journeys more likely. Construction and the need to extend services also use materials and energy.
clean_electricity: Power produced with little release of gases that warm the planet. It can help cut pollution when it replaces fossil-fuel power or supplies transport and heating. Its wider effects still depend on how equipment is built, where it is placed and how the grid operates.
coal_retirement: Closing power stations that burn coal for good, and replacing the power they provide. This can cut air pollution and releases of carbon dioxide. The change also needs a reliable new power supply and support for workers and local people.
renewable_energy_deployment: Building and using power sources such as wind and sunlight that are naturally replenished. They can replace electricity made from fossil fuels. Grids, storage and careful siting help make that replacement reliable and limit damage to nearby communities and habitats.
grid_scale_storage: Saving energy for use later across an electricity network. Batteries and other systems can supply power when production is low or demand is high. This helps balance supply and demand, although different technologies store different amounts for different lengths of time.
demand_response: Changing when electricity is used to ease pressure on the power system. For example, suitable equipment can run earlier or later instead of during the busiest hours. This can reduce the need to start additional power plants, provided essential needs are protected.
methane_leak_detection: Finding and fixing places where a powerful heat-trapping gas escapes from equipment. Sensors, inspections, aircraft and satellites can help locate leaks. Reducing releases depends on repairs being completed and checked, not just on spotting them.
refrigerant_phase_down: Gradually replacing cooling gases that have a strong warming effect with alternatives that have a smaller one. Preventing leaks and recovering gases from old equipment are also important. The aim is to reduce climate pollution while keeping cooling safe and accessible.
carbon_dioxide_removal: Taking a heat-trapping gas out of the air and storing it in plants, soils, rocks or other reservoirs. The benefit depends on how much is removed and how long it stays stored. This has limits and does not replace the need to reduce new releases.
building_energy_efficiency: Using less power or fuel to keep indoor spaces comfortable and useful. Better insulation, windows, lighting and appliances can provide the same services with less energy. Results depend on installation, maintenance and how the building is used.
heat_pump_electrification: Replacing fuel-burning heating with electrical equipment that transfers warmth between places. The same type of equipment can also provide cooling. The climate benefit depends on its efficiency, the equipment it replaces and how the electricity is produced.
weatherization_retrofits: Improving existing homes so outdoor heat, cold and moisture are easier to manage. Work can include sealing gaps, adding insulation and improving shade. Suitable ventilation is also needed to keep indoor air healthy.
passive_cooling_design: Keeping indoor spaces cooler through their design before relying on powered cooling. Shade, airflow, reflective roofs and carefully chosen materials can help. The best combination depends on local weather and the building's use.
building_performance_standards: Rules requiring buildings to meet limits on actual energy use or pollution over time. Owners may need to improve equipment or the building itself. Measuring real results helps show whether those improvements work.
public_transit_expansion: Adding or improving shared transport such as buses and trains. Frequent, reliable services can help people reach work, school and health care with fewer private car journeys. Benefits depend on access, affordability and the energy used.
active_mobility: Creating safe, connected routes for journeys on foot, by wheelchair or by bicycle. These routes can replace some short car trips and make daily destinations easier to reach. Accessibility and protection from traffic are essential.
electric_vehicle_transition: Replacing vehicles that burn fuel with ones powered by electricity. This reduces exhaust pollution on the road, while the overall climate benefit depends on electricity and manufacturing. It does not by itself solve congestion or reduce the need for roads.
low_carbon_cement: Reducing the gases released when making the materials used to bind and form concrete. Approaches include using less material, changing ingredients and using cleaner heat. The result must still meet the strength and safety needs of the structure.
green_steel: Making the iron-based metal used in buildings and cars while releasing much less carbon dioxide. Factories can recycle more metal, use cleaner power or change how they process iron ore. The amount saved depends on the fuel, power and materials used.
ecosystem_restoration: Helping damaged natural places recover their plants, animals and important functions. This can improve water, soil, wildlife habitat and carbon storage. Recovery is more likely to last when the original causes of damage are also addressed.
multi_hazard_early_warning: Alerting people in time to prepare for threats such as floods, storms or dangerous heat. A forecast only helps if the warning reaches people, is understood and can be acted on. Safe places, transport and response plans matter too.
urban_heat_action_plans: Preparing a city to protect people before and during dangerously hot weather. Measures can include warnings, worker protection, shade, outreach and places to cool down. Plans need to reach people who have the fewest ways to protect themselves.
equitable_cooling_access: Making sure people can keep safely cool, including those with low incomes or unsuitable housing. This can involve shade, better homes, affordable electricity and public cool spaces. Reliable power and efficient equipment help keep protection available during extreme heat.
flood_resilient_infrastructure: Designing or improving buildings, roads, drains and utilities so they can better withstand high water. Measures can reduce damage and help services recover. They need to reflect local conditions and the possibility of floods larger than those seen in the past.
water_reuse: Cleaning used water so it can serve another purpose. Depending on the treatment, it may be used for farming, industry or drinking supplies. Health safeguards and reliable treatment are needed, and the process also uses energy.
climate_resilient_agriculture: Helping farms keep producing under changing heat, rainfall, pests and other pressures. Options include varied crops, healthier soil, careful water use and better forecasts. The best choices depend on local conditions and farmers' resources.
planned_relocation: Organizing a move away from places that cannot be kept acceptably safe. A fair process protects people's choices, homes, livelihoods and community ties. It also requires suitable land, services and support at the destination.
nature_based_adaptation: Using healthy natural places to help people cope with climate hazards. Wetlands can hold floodwater, trees can provide shade, and coastal habitats can soften waves. Their protection has limits and depends on keeping those natural systems healthy.
aquifer_overdraft: Pumping water from an underground store faster than it is replaced. Water levels can fall, making wells less reliable. In some places, continued pumping can also pull salty water into supplies used for drinking or farming.
river_flow_regime_shift: A lasting change in how much water a river carries, when it carries it or how variable the flow is. Earlier snowmelt or longer dry periods can change the usual seasonal pattern. This affects water supplies, wildlife and the management of dams.
reservoir_storage_instability: The amount of usable water held behind a dam becoming less predictable. A reservoir may fill at unexpected times or have too little water when it is needed. This makes it harder to plan drinking supplies, farming and electricity generation.
reservoir_operating_shortfall: A dam's stored water or ability to release it falling short of what people expect it to provide. Operators may be unable to meet water supply, electricity or flood-control needs. Competing demands and the timing of incoming water affect the result.
snowmelt_timing_shift: Snow melting at a different time of year or at a different pace from the usual pattern. This changes when water reaches rivers and reservoirs. Earlier melting can leave less stored snow to supply water later in the warm season.
soil_moisture_collapse: A large drop in the water held in soil. Plants then have less water available to their roots, and the land can dry out further during hot weather. How serious the effects are depends on soil depth, vegetation and how long the shortage lasts.
flash_flood_regime: The pattern of floods that rise very quickly after intense rain or a sudden release of water. Their speed can leave little time to respond. Damage depends on where the water travels and whether people, buildings and roads are in its path.
drought_persistence: Unusually dry conditions continuing for many months or across several seasons. Soil, rivers and reservoirs may not recover between dry periods. The effects build up when each new season begins with less water in reserve.
freshwater_lens_compression: The layer of usable fresh water beneath a small island becoming thinner. This water sits above denser salty water. Too much pumping, little rain or seawater entering the ground can reduce the amount available for wells.
drinking_water_treatment_stress: Water-cleaning systems having more difficulty making supplies safe to drink. Salt, dirt, harmful germs or other pollutants can require extra treatment or exceed what equipment can handle. This can increase costs or interrupt supply.
watershed_forest_loss: Trees being removed or dying in the area that drains into a river or lake. Without their cover and roots, rain can carry more soil into the water. Water quality and the timing of flows can change.
wastewater_infrastructure_overflow: Used water escaping from sewers, pumps or treatment plants because the system cannot contain it. Heavy rain, equipment failure or blocked drainage can contribute. The spilled water may carry pollutants and disease-causing germs into nearby areas.
wastewater_bypass_discharge: Used water being released without passing through all the cleaning steps it would normally receive. This can happen during overloads, breakdowns or maintenance. The receiving river or coastal water may then receive more pollutants.
irrigation_water_inefficiency: Water supplied to crops being lost or poorly timed, so it does not provide the intended benefit. Leaks, evaporation and excess watering can contribute. Effects on the wider water supply depend on whether unused water returns in a usable form.
hydropower_reliability_decline: Electricity made from moving water becoming less dependable. Too little water, poorly timed flows or limits on dam releases can reduce generation when it is needed. The effects depend on the river and how the power system is managed.
basin_treaty_breakdown: Agreements about sharing a river's water becoming harder to follow or enforce. Drought, changing flows and competing needs can strain cooperation between regions or countries. The result depends on the agreement and the ability to resolve disputes.
desalination_dependence: Relying on equipment that removes salt from water because other supplies are limited or unreliable. This can provide usable water, but it needs energy, maintenance and safe management of the concentrated salt left over. A breakdown can threaten supply where alternatives are scarce.
ice_sheet_mass_loss: The vast ice covering Greenland or Antarctica losing more ice than it gains from snowfall. Melting and the movement of ice into the ocean both contribute. Losing ice that was on land adds water to the sea.
glacial_lake_failure_risk: The chance that a lake held back by ice or loose rock near a glacier suddenly releases its water. If that barrier fails, a fast flood can rush downhill. The danger depends on the lake, the barrier and what lies downstream.
sea_ice_season_loss: A region of ocean staying frozen for a shorter part of the year. Ice may form later or melt earlier. This changes conditions for wildlife, coastal protection and travel. The area covered in one month does not tell us the full season's length.
coastal_inundation_risk: How likely seawater is to spread onto nearby land, and how serious the flooding could be. Storms can push water inland, while high tides and rising sea levels make it easier for water to reach homes, roads and other low-lying places.
thermokarst_expansion: More land sinking or becoming uneven as ice inside frozen ground melts. The changes can create ponds, damage structures and alter drainage. Wet, thawed plant material can also decay and release gases that warm the planet.
arctic_shipping_expansion: More vessels travelling through northern polar waters, or using them for a longer season. Less sea ice can open routes, but moving ice, severe weather and limited ports still create hazards. Less ice alone does not guarantee more vessel traffic.
polar_infrastructure_failure: Roads, buildings, power supplies or other essential structures in polar regions becoming unable to do their job. Thawing ground, erosion and severe conditions can cause damage. Remote locations can make repairs and replacement supplies difficult.
snow_drought: Less water being stored as seasonal snow than usual. This can happen because too little snow falls, more precipitation falls as rain, or snow melts early. Rivers and reservoirs may then receive less water during the season when it is needed.
firn_layer_depletion: Older, partly compressed snow losing the small spaces that can hold meltwater. If these spaces fill with ice or disappear, less water can be stored or frozen again. More meltwater may then drain off an ice sheet.
glacier_meltwater_dependency: People and natural systems relying on water released by melting mountain ice. That water can be especially important during dry seasons. As glaciers shrink, the timing and long-term reliability of this supply can change.
oceanic_deoxygenation: Seawater losing some of the oxygen that marine animals need to live. Warming and changes in water mixing can contribute. Animals may have less suitable living space, particularly where oxygen was already scarce.
antarctic_bottom_water_decline: Less cold, dense water forming near Antarctica and sinking to the deepest ocean. This movement helps renew deep water and carry oxygen into it. A reduction can change conditions far below the surface.
ocean_acidification: Seawater becoming more acidic as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air. The chemical change makes some of the materials used to build shells and coral skeletons less available. The ocean does not need to become an acid overall for these effects to matter.
pacific_decadal_oscillation: A broad pattern of warmer and cooler surface waters in the North Pacific that varies over years and decades. It is linked to changes in regional rainfall and marine conditions. It describes natural climate variability rather than a simple rise in temperature everywhere.
atlantic_multidecadal_oscillation: A pattern of changes in North Atlantic surface temperatures over several decades. It is associated with shifts in regional climate and ocean conditions. The pattern alone does not show which changes were caused by people or predict conditions in a particular place.
atlantic_ni_o_ni_a: Warmer or cooler than usual surface waters in the tropical Atlantic, especially near the equator. These changes interact with winds and can shift rainfall nearby and farther away. This is a distinct pattern from the better-known warm and cool phases in the tropical Pacific.
indian_ocean_dipole: A difference in surface temperature between the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean that becomes stronger or reverses. This contrast changes winds and where rain tends to fall. Its effects depend on the season and other climate patterns happening at the same time.
marine_fisheries_collapse: Fish populations becoming so depleted that they can no longer support normal catches or their usual role in the sea. Fishing pressure, habitat damage and environmental changes can contribute. Recovery depends on the species and whether the pressures are reduced.
fish_landing_supply_disruption: Caught seafood failing to reach ports, processing facilities or markets as reliably as expected. Changes in catches, damaged ports or transport problems can interrupt supply. Communities that rely heavily on fish for food or income may be especially affected.
ocean_current_regime_shift: A lasting change in the direction, strength, depth or seasonal timing of moving seawater. These movements carry heat, nutrients and marine organisms. A change can therefore affect conditions far from the place where it starts.
coastal_hypoxia: Water near the shore containing too little oxygen for many animals to live normally. Warm water, limited mixing and the decay of excess algae can contribute. Fish may leave the area, while animals unable to move can be harmed.
marine_food_web_simplification: Changes in which sea creatures eat which, and in how energy passes between them. Some species or feeding links may disappear while others become more common. This can change fish catches and make the system less able to cope with further disturbance.
ocean_salinity_stratification: Seawater forming layers because some water is saltier and denser than the water above it. Stronger separation can make the layers mix less easily. This affects how oxygen, heat, nutrients and carbon move between shallow and deep water.
harmful_algal_blooms: Rapid growth of tiny water-living organisms that can make toxins, block light or use up oxygen as they decay. Not every outbreak has all of these effects. Harmful episodes can kill aquatic animals or make seafood unsafe to harvest.
pelagic_species_redistribution: Animals that live in open water moving to different places, depths or seasonal feeding areas. Changes in temperature, food and oxygen can help drive these movements. Predators, prey and fishing communities may no longer find them where they used to.
littoral_surge_vulnerability: People, buildings and natural habitats lying in the path of seawater pushed ashore by storms. The same storm can cause different damage depending on the shore, water level and protection in place. High tides, waves and rain can add to the danger.
land_carbon_sink_weakening: Plants and soils taking up less carbon dioxide than they otherwise would. Heat, drought and other disturbances can reduce this natural help in slowing warming. Less uptake does not necessarily mean the land has become a net source of the gas.
peat_oxidation_pulse: A burst of carbon release when long-stored, partly decayed plant material is exposed to air and breaks down. Draining or drying the ground can allow this to happen. Carbon that accumulated over a long time can then return to the atmosphere.
tidal_wetland_carbon_reversal: Coastal habitats changing from storing carbon to releasing some of their stored carbon. Damage, drainage or loss of vegetation can expose buried plant material to decay. The outcome depends on the habitat and what happens to its soil or sediment.
ocean_carbon_uptake_weakening: The sea absorbing less carbon dioxide than it otherwise would. Temperature, chemistry and water circulation affect how much it can take up. Reduced absorption leaves more of the gas in the air, even if the ocean still absorbs carbon overall.
nocturnal_heat_stress: Nights staying hot enough to make recovery from daytime heat difficult. Homes may remain warm and people may struggle to cool down or rest. The effect depends on humidity, housing, health and access to cooling.
compound_day_night_heat_extremes: Very hot days followed by nights that also stay unusually hot. The cooler hours that normally provide relief are missing. Continued exposure can put more strain on people and increase the need for cooling across both day and night.
hail_hazard_shift: Changes in where, when or how severely storms produce damaging balls of ice. Storm strength, moisture and the height at which water freezes all matter. A change may increase damage in some places without increasing it everywhere.
madden_julian_oscillation: A large area of clouds, rain and changing winds that travels eastward through the tropics over several weeks. Its passage can make some regions wetter and others drier. It can also influence storms and weather far beyond the tropics.
north_atlantic_oscillation: Changes in the air-pressure contrast across the North Atlantic that influence winds and storm routes. Different phases can bring different winter temperature and rainfall patterns to surrounding regions. It is a recurring pattern of variability, not a forecast for every local weather event.
arctic_oscillation: Changes in air pressure between the Arctic and regions farther south. These changes influence winds and the routes taken by storms and cold air. Their effects vary by region and interact with other weather patterns.
pacific_north_american_pattern: A recurring arrangement of high and low air pressure over the Pacific Ocean and North America. It helps steer storms and changes where warm or cold air moves. Different phases can alter temperature and rainfall across the continent.
southern_annular_mode: The belt of strong westerly winds around Antarctica shifting north or south. This changes storm routes, rainfall and conditions in the surrounding ocean. Effects differ between places and seasons.
quasi_biennial_oscillation: Winds high above the equator switching between easterly and westerly directions roughly every couple of years. These changes occur well above most ordinary weather. They can influence how air moves through the wider atmosphere.
blocking_pattern_persistence: A large area of high air pressure staying in place and slowing the usual movement of weather systems. The same conditions can linger over a region. Depending on the season and location, this can prolong heat, cold or dry weather.
humidity_amplification: More water vapour being present in the air. Warmer air can hold more moisture, although the amount available varies by place. Extra moisture can make heat harder to tolerate and provide more water for heavy rain.
lightning_fire_weather: Lightning hitting vegetation when it is dry enough to catch and sustain a fire. A strike does not always start a wildfire. Dry fuel, wind, rainfall and the response to a new fire help determine what happens next.
atmospheric_dryness: How strongly the surrounding air and weather conditions draw water out of soil, plants and open water. Heat, low humidity, wind and sunlight can increase this drying effect. Water shortages grow when rain cannot replace what is lost.
soot_deposition_on_snow: Dark particles from burning fuel or vegetation settling on snow. Darker snow reflects less sunlight and absorbs more heat, which can speed up melting. The effect depends on the amount of particles and the condition of the snow.
ozone_formation_pressure: Hot, sunny or still weather making it easier for certain air pollutants to react and form a harmful gas near the ground. This can worsen air quality even without an increase in the gases that start the reactions. Local chemistry and wind conditions matter.
rossby_wave_stalling: Large bends in high-altitude winds moving slowly or remaining in a similar pattern. This can help keep the same weather over a region for longer. Whether it leads to heat, cold, rain or drought depends on the position of the bends.
smoke_exposure_burden: The harm and disruption caused when people breathe smoke from fires or other burning. Effects depend on the pollution level and how long exposure lasts. Health, housing and access to cleaner indoor air influence who is most affected.
low_cloud_deck_retreat: Low clouds over the sea covering less area or lasting for less time. These clouds reflect some sunlight back into space. Losing them can let the ocean absorb more sunlight in the affected region.
aerosol_cooling_loss: A reduction in the cooling influence of some tiny particles suspended in the air. These particles can reflect sunlight or change clouds. As that cooling decreases, more of the warming from heat-trapping gases can become apparent. This does not make air pollution beneficial overall.
grid_peak_load_stress: Electricity use approaching or exceeding what power plants, wires and other equipment can supply during busy periods. Very hot weather can increase demand for cooling while also straining equipment. The system may need extra supply, reduced demand or temporary restrictions.
peaker_plant_lock_in: Continuing to rely on power stations that burn fuel mainly at the busiest times of day. Old equipment, contracts and the need for backup power can make change hard. These stations still release pollution, even if they run for only a few hours.
transmission_buildout_lag: New electricity lines and network upgrades taking longer to arrive than they are needed. Planning, approvals, financing or construction can cause delays. This can slow the connection of cleaner power and new equipment that needs electricity.
transformer_supply_bottleneck: Too few of the devices that change electricity from one voltage to another being available when needed. These devices are essential for connecting and repairing power networks. Long waits can delay upgrades or recovery after damage.
gas_power_dependence: An electricity system relying heavily on stations that burn natural gas. This ties supply to fuel availability and price and continues to release carbon dioxide. Alternatives depend on the power network, other generation and ways to balance demand.
industrial_heat_decarbonization_gap: The remaining work needed to replace fossil fuels used to produce heat in factories. Some processes require very high temperatures or new equipment. Cleaner options can be limited by cost, technology and access to suitable energy supplies.
cement_process_emissions: Carbon dioxide released when limestone is chemically changed to make the binding ingredient in concrete. This release comes from the material itself. It is separate from the carbon dioxide released by burning fuel to heat the kiln.
steel_decarbonization_gap: The distance between today's metal-making methods and widespread use of methods that release much less carbon dioxide. Coal-based equipment can remain in service for many years. Replacing it may require cleaner electricity, different raw materials and major investment.
critical_mineral_extraction_pressure: Growing demand for batteries, electronics and electricity networks driving more mining and processing. This can increase competition for land and water and create more waste. The effects depend on the minerals, location and safeguards.
battery_supply_chain_pressure: Growing demand for materials used to store power in phones, cars and other equipment. These materials must be mined, processed and moved to factories. Fast growth can strain supplies and add damage near mines and factories. Recycling and the way workers are treated also matter.
semiconductor_fabrication_footprint: The resources used and pollution produced while making electronic chips. Factories need electricity, highly purified water and specialized chemicals. The size of these effects depends on the manufacturing process and local energy and water supplies.
cooling_water_competition: Power stations, computing facilities and other users needing water from the same limited supply to remove heat. This can compete with household, farming and river needs. The effect depends on how much water is consumed, returned and available locally.
backup_generator_dependence: Relying on on-site engines to provide electricity when the main supply fails or is insufficient. Engines that burn diesel or gas release air pollution and carbon dioxide. The effect depends on how often they run and what they replace.
energy_affordability_crisis: Households or essential services being unable to reliably pay for the power or fuel they need. People may have to cut back on heating, cooling or other necessities. The problem depends on prices, income, housing and available support.
utility_disconnection_risk: The chance of losing access to a service such as electricity, including when bills cannot be paid. Losing power can also stop cooling and other essential equipment. The consequences depend on the service, duration and the household's needs.
renewable_curtailment_losses: Available wind or solar electricity being deliberately left unused because the system cannot accept it at that time. Limited power lines, storage or demand can contribute. The cost and climate effects depend on how the wider electricity system operates.
aviation_demand_growth: More passenger journeys or freight being carried by aircraft. Additional flying can increase fuel use and demand for airports and equipment. The total effect depends on aircraft efficiency, fuel and changes in the routes flown.
shipping_lane_disruption: Routes used by commercial vessels becoming difficult or impossible to use. Closures, low water, storms or other obstacles can cause delays and detours. This can interrupt deliveries and raise transport costs.
freight_electrification_gap: The remaining work needed to replace fuel-burning goods transport with electric vehicles and equipment. Vehicles alone are not enough: charging, reliable power and suitable operating plans are also needed. Limits in any of these can slow the transition.
port_heat_vulnerability: Harbour workers, equipment and stored goods being susceptible to damage or disruption during very hot weather. Heat can limit safe work and strain cooling systems. Effects depend on local conditions and the protection available.
road_freight_diesel_lock_in: Trucks and delivery networks remaining dependent on diesel fuel. Long-lived vehicles, refuelling systems and business arrangements can make switching difficult. Continued fuel burning produces carbon dioxide and harmful air pollution.
airport_climate_exposure: Runways, terminals, workers and access routes being in places affected by hazards such as floods or extreme heat. Exposure describes what can encounter the hazard. Actual disruption also depends on protection, preparation and the event's severity.
airport_operational_disruption: Flights, ground services or passenger movements being delayed or stopped. Heavy rain, heat or damaged equipment can contribute. Effects may spread to other places when aircraft, staff or cargo cannot continue their journeys.
bridge_scour_exposure: Flowing water being able to wash away soil or rock around a bridge's supports. Losing this material can weaken the foundations. The risk depends on river flow, the riverbed and the design and condition of the bridge.
rail_heat_buckling: Train tracks bending out of position as the metal expands in hot weather. Where that expansion is constrained, forces can build up in the rails. Inspections, slower trains or closures may be needed to keep services safe.
biodiversity_intactness_loss: An area's original mix and abundance of living things declining compared with a reference condition. Some species may disappear while others become much less common. The measure concerns the wider living community, rather than just counting how many species remain.
wildfire_regime_shift: Changes in how often fires occur, when they burn, how intense they are or how much land they affect. Weather, vegetation and human activity all influence these patterns. A change can affect habitats, communities and smoke exposure.
forest_fragmentation: A large wooded area being broken into smaller, separated patches. Roads, clearing and other disturbances can make it harder for wildlife to move between them. Effects depend on the species and whether the spaces between patches can be crossed.
mangrove_buffer_loss: The loss of coastal trees and roots that help soften waves and hold shorelines together. Nearby communities can become more exposed to water and erosion. These habitats also support wildlife and store carbon.
reef_structural_collapse: The hard framework built by corals breaking down faster than it is maintained. This removes shelter for marine life and can reduce protection from waves. Heat damage and conditions that hinder skeleton growth can contribute.
pollinator_service_decline: Bees and other animals becoming less able to transfer pollen between flowers. Many plants need this help to produce seeds or fruit. The effects depend on the crops or wild plants involved and what other pollinating species remain.
freshwater_ecosystem_collapse: Rivers, lakes or wetlands losing much of their living community or their ability to function. Pollution, altered flows and barriers can contribute. The term describes severe damage, not simply any change in a waterway.
species_range_compression: The area where a plant or animal can live becoming smaller. Conditions may become unsuitable at one edge while barriers prevent movement into better areas. Smaller living areas can make populations more vulnerable to further disturbance.
insect_biomass_decline: A reduction in the total mass of insects in a defined place and period. This can reflect fewer insects, smaller insects or changes in which kinds are present. It can affect animals that eat insects and the work insects do in natural systems.
soil_humus_decline: Soil losing the well-decayed plant and animal material that helps it hold water and nutrients. Erosion and changes in land management can contribute. With less of this material, soil can become less able to support plants during dry conditions.
urban_tree_canopy_loss: A city losing the cover provided by tree leaves and branches. Streets and buildings receive less shade, and less water is released by trees to cool the air. The loss can make already hot neighbourhoods harder to keep cool.
crop_yield_volatility: Harvest amounts changing more unpredictably between seasons or places. Heat, water shortages, heavy rain and other pressures can contribute. This makes planning food supplies and farm income harder, even when average production has not fallen.
farm_heat_stress: Hot conditions making agricultural work harder or less safe. Physical effort, humidity and long hours can add to the strain. Reduced safe working time can affect both workers' health and the work needed to produce food.
livestock_disease_pressure: Conditions making farm animals more likely to become ill. Germs, biting insects, heat, crowding and care practices can all matter. Illness can reduce production, cause deaths or require restrictions on animal movement.
fertilizer_price_shock: A sudden rise in the cost of products used to supply crops with nutrients. Farmers may face higher bills or use less, affecting later harvests. The result depends on crop needs, other available nutrients and farmers' finances.
feed_crop_dependency: Animal farming relying on dedicated supplies of crops such as maize and soy. Producing that feed uses land, water and other resources. Poor harvests or supply interruptions can then raise costs or limit livestock production.
food_import_exposure: A place relying on food brought in from elsewhere, leaving it affected by problems beyond its borders. Poor harvests, trade restrictions or transport delays can change availability and prices. The effect depends on alternative suppliers and local reserves.
cold_chain_failure_risk: The chance that food or other temperature-sensitive goods become too warm during storage or transport. A power cut, equipment fault or delay can break the required cooling. Goods may spoil before reaching the people who need them.
fishery_protein_dependence: People relying heavily on fish and other harvested seafood for nourishment. If catches or access decline, suitable replacement foods may be costly or unavailable. The effects depend on local diets, incomes and alternatives.
agricultural_labor_exposure: Farm workers coming into contact with hazards such as heat, smoke and chemicals. The type of task and time spent working affect the dose or strain they receive. Protection, rest and access to services influence the resulting harm.
topsoil_erosion_acceleration: The fertile upper layer of soil being removed faster by water, wind or farming activities. This carries away material that holds nutrients and water. Plants can become harder to grow, and the displaced soil can enter nearby waterways.
insurance_retreat: Insurers reducing the cover they offer, raising prices or leaving markets where losses are difficult to manage. Repeated climate-related damage can contribute. Households and businesses may then have fewer affordable ways to protect themselves financially.
mortgage_market_exposure: Home loans, borrowers and lenders being vulnerable to damage, falling property values or loss of insurance. Repeated hazards can make a property more costly to own or harder to sell. These effects depend on local markets and lending arrangements.
public_health_heat_burden: The combined illness, deaths and demand for care associated with dangerously hot conditions. Hospitals and support services may face extra pressure at the same time. Housing, income, health and access to cooling influence who is most affected.
vector_borne_disease_expansion: Illnesses carried by insects or other animals becoming able to spread in new places or seasons. Temperature and moisture affect the carriers and the germs they carry. Suitable conditions alone do not guarantee an outbreak. Exposure and public-health protection matter too.
adaptation_capital_shortfall: Too little funding being available to prepare for climate hazards and reduce their damage. Projects such as safer housing, drainage or cooling may be delayed. A funding gap is different from proving that any particular project will work.
critical_infrastructure_fragility: Essential systems such as electricity, water and transport being easily disrupted or slow to recover. Damage in one system can interrupt others that depend on it. Maintenance, backup capacity and local hazards affect how fragile the network is.
disaster_recovery_inequality: People having unequal chances to rebuild after a damaging event. Those with less money, insurance, secure housing or access to aid may take longer to recover. Repeated losses can leave them with fewer resources to prepare for the next event.
relocation_governance_capacity: The ability of public institutions to organize and support a fair move away from unsafe places. This includes planning, funding, community choice and protection of rights. Suitable housing, services and livelihoods are needed at the destination.
climate_litigation_pressure: Lawsuits creating demands to address climate-related harm, pollution or failures to prepare. Cases can raise questions about responsibility, disclosure and funding. Their outcomes depend on the legal setting and the evidence in each case.
conflict_risk_escalation: Conditions making disputes or violence more likely or harder to resolve. Climate hazards can worsen existing pressures through lost livelihoods, food shortages or displacement. They are one possible influence among many, not a direct or inevitable cause of conflict.
talik_expansion: Unfrozen areas inside or beneath otherwise frozen ground becoming larger. These areas can let water move through places that were previously blocked by ice. Where thawed plant material and low-oxygen conditions occur, they can also enable releases of methane.
pollinator_colony_collapse: A community of bees or other pollinating insects losing so many members that it can no longer function normally. Disease, parasites, poor nutrition, chemicals and weather can contribute. Losing colonies can reduce the help that nearby plants receive in producing seeds and fruit.
nitrogen_fertilizer_runoff: Rain or irrigation carrying unused crop nutrients off fields into drains, rivers and lakes. Those nutrients can encourage excessive algae growth. The effects depend on the amount reaching the water and the conditions there.
tropospheric_ozone: A reactive gas in the lower atmosphere that forms when other pollutants react in sunlight. Near the ground it can harm lungs and plants, and it also traps heat. It is distinct from the protective layer of the same gas much higher in the atmosphere.
marine_heatwaves: Seawater staying unusually warm for a prolonged period compared with the normal conditions for that place and season. This can stress corals, fish and other marine life. The effects depend on how hot the water becomes, how long it stays warm and which species are present.
fracking_wastewater_lakes: Ponds used to hold contaminated water from operations that extract oil or gas by fracturing rock. Leaks, spills or poor handling can threaten nearby water supplies. The risks depend on the stored material, site and protection in place.
cattle_grazing_overcompaction: Repeated movement of farm animals pressing soil together so tightly that it loses spaces for air and water. This can make it harder for roots to grow and rain to soak in. The effect depends on animal numbers, soil conditions and how grazing is managed.
nitrous_oxide: A long-lasting gas that traps heat in the atmosphere. It is released by natural processes and human activities, particularly where soil microbes process added nutrients or manure. It contributes to warming alongside other heat-trapping gases.
phytoplankton_decline: A reduction in the tiny drifting organisms that use sunlight to grow in water. They support many marine food chains. Changes in their abundance or growth can affect the animals that feed on them and, later, fish catches.
antarctic_shelf_instability: Floating platforms of ice around Antarctica thinning, cracking or retreating. These platforms help hold back ice flowing from land. When their support weakens, some inland ice can move toward the sea more quickly.
wildlife_habitat_patches: Separate pieces of land or water where wild plants and animals can live. Their size, quality and connections influence whether populations can find food, shelter and mates. A patch may remain present while becoming too isolated for some species.
topsoil_salinization_fields: Salt building up in the upper soil where crops grow. Excess salt can make it harder for roots to take in water and can damage soil structure. The effect depends on the crop, water supply and drainage.
staple_food_price_volatility: The cost of everyday foods such as rice, wheat or maize swinging sharply or unpredictably. This makes household spending and farm planning harder. People with low incomes or few reserves may struggle when prices rise.
sulfur_dioxide: A gas released by burning sulfur-containing fuels, processing some metals and volcanic activity. It can harm air quality and form tiny particles that reflect sunlight. Reducing the gas improves air quality while also changing that short-lived cooling influence.
coral_bleaching: Stressed corals losing the tiny algae that live inside them and supply much of their food. The corals become pale and have less energy. They may recover if conditions improve, so turning white does not necessarily mean they have died.
invasive_species_encroachment: Plants, animals or other organisms spreading outside their native range and causing harm. They can crowd out local species or change habitats and feeding relationships. Not every species introduced to a new place becomes harmful.
deepwater_petroleum_spill_risk: Oil and gas operations far below the sea surface. High pressure, distance from shore and difficult access can make accidents harder to prevent or manage. Released oil can harm marine life, depending on where it spreads and how long exposure lasts.
volatile_organic_compounds: Carbon-containing chemicals that readily enter the air as gases. Sources include fuels, solvents, plants and industrial processes. Some are harmful to breathe or take part in reactions that produce other air pollution.
sea_level_rise: The average height of the ocean increasing over time. Warming makes seawater expand, while melting ice on land adds more water. Local changes also depend on currents and whether the land itself is rising or sinking.
tundra_methane_outgassing: A heat-trapping gas escaping from cold northern soils, wetlands and lakes. Microbes can produce it when thawed plant material decays with little oxygen. The amount released depends on both production and processes that break the gas down before it reaches the air.
soil_microbial_depletion: Soil losing some of its tiny living organisms or their ability to do useful work. These organisms help break down material and make nutrients available to plants. Compaction, chemicals and changing water conditions can affect them.
surface_water_storage_instability: Water held in lakes and reservoirs becoming less predictable or reliable. Changing inflows, evaporation and withdrawals can cause larger swings. These changes matter most where users have little spare supply to cope with a low-water period.
pesticide_bioaccumulation_chains: Long-lasting pest-control chemicals remaining in bottom sediments or inside living things. Repeated exposure can allow some chemicals to build up in tissues or pass through food chains. Effects depend on the chemical, dose and species.
pm2_5_particulates: Tiny airborne particles no wider than 2.5 micrometres, much smaller than the width of a human hair. They can reach deep into the lungs when breathed in. Their health effects depend on concentration, composition and the length of exposure.
anoxic_dead_zones: Areas of coastal water with too little oxygen for many fish and bottom-dwelling animals. Excess nutrients can fuel algae growth whose decay uses up oxygen. Some animals leave, while those that cannot move may die.
ice_albedo_feedback_loops: A cycle in which melting snow or ice exposes darker land or water. The darker surface absorbs more sunlight, causing more warming and further melting. This can strengthen an initial temperature increase.
forest_dieback_areas: Wooded landscapes where many trees are dying because they cannot recover from the pressures they face. Drought, heat, pests and fire can combine. The effects depend on which trees are lost and whether the forest can regrow.
combined_sewer_overflow: Rainwater and sewage spilling out of a shared pipe system when it becomes too full. The released mixture may not receive normal treatment. This can carry pollution and germs into nearby rivers or coastal waters.
humanitarian_resource_gaps: The difference between the help people need in a crisis and what aid services can actually deliver. Staff, money, supplies, transport or access may be insufficient. A promise of funding alone does not ensure that help reaches people.
carbon_monoxide: A poisonous, colourless gas produced when fuels do not burn completely. Breathing it reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. The danger depends on the concentration, time exposed and the person's health and activity.
gulf_stream_slowdown: Changes in the strength and route of the powerful current carrying warm water through the western North Atlantic. Its movement affects regional ocean conditions and nearby coastal water levels. This current is related to, but is not the same as, the entire Atlantic overturning circulation.
hydrological_runoff_surges: Water suddenly flowing off land or out of melting snow into streams much faster than usual. Rapid flows can carry soil and pollutants and raise river levels. The outcome depends on the landscape, ground conditions and drainage.
floodplain_exposure: People, homes, roads and other assets located on land that a river can cover when it overflows. Being in this area creates potential exposure. Actual damage depends on the flood and the protection in place.
groundwater_depletion_wells: Wells reaching less usable water because the underground water level has fallen. Continued pumping can lower levels faster than they recover. A well may become more expensive to use or stop supplying water altogether.
solar_radiation_trapping: The extra heat kept in Earth's climate system by gases such as carbon dioxide and methane. These gases reduce how easily heat escapes to space. When more energy stays in than leaves, the land and oceans warm as the system adjusts.
ocean_heat_content: The amount of heat stored in seawater within a stated depth and area. It describes more than the temperature at the surface. As the sea stores more heat, the water can expand and conditions for marine life can change.
peatland_degradations: Damage to wet ground that contains deep stores of partly decayed plant material. Draining or drying it lets that material break down more quickly. This can release stored carbon, lower the ground surface and damage wildlife habitat.
waterborne_pathogen_outbreaks: Groups of people getting sick after contact with water that contains harmful germs. People may drink the water, swim in it or touch it during a flood. The risk depends on which germs are present and whether water and sewage systems keep people safe.
emergency_response_overload: More people needing urgent help than available staff, vehicles, beds or equipment can serve in time. Several problems can happen at once during a disaster. Delays depend on both the size of the emergency and the resources available locally.
zoonotic_disease_outbreaks: Clusters of illness caused by germs that can pass between animals and people. An outbreak may require both human and animal health services. Its spread depends on the germ, contacts and measures used to detect and contain it.
coastal_erosion: Waves, currents and storms wearing away the land at the sea's edge. Beaches, cliffs and wetlands can lose material. Homes, roads and habitats may become more exposed as the shoreline moves inland.
alpine_snowpack_declines: Mountain snow becoming thinner, covering less area, holding less water or lasting for a shorter time. Warming can turn some snowfall into rain and bring earlier melting. This changes the water stored for later in the year.
wetlands_drainage_scales: Removing or redirecting water from naturally wet land. This changes the plants and animals that can live there and can reduce natural floodwater storage. Where the soil contains long-stored plant material, drying can also release carbon.
subsea_cable_landing_chokepoint: Many undersea communication lines reaching land through a small number of coastal sites. Shared power or onward connections can create a common weak point. Damage at one such site may interrupt several routes at once.
rice_paddy_methane_bubbles: A heat-trapping gas being released as plant material breaks down in flooded crop fields with little oxygen. It can escape through plants, bubbles or the water surface. Releases depend on water management, soil and the growing season.
managed_retreat_pressure: A growing need to decide whether staying in a hazardous place is still safe or affordable. Repeated flooding or erosion may make protection and rebuilding increasingly difficult. Decisions involve homes, livelihoods, public costs and community choice.
jet_stream_volatility: Changes in the position, speed or bends of the fast-moving winds high in the atmosphere. These winds help guide weather systems. Large or slow-moving bends can contribute to conditions lingering over a region.
glacier_calving_events: Chunks of ice breaking away from the edge of a glacier into a lake or the sea. This forms icebergs and removes ice from the glacier. Large events can also disturb nearby water and create local hazards.
wildfire_smoke_hospitalization_burden: Hospital admissions linked to breathing pollution from vegetation fires. These admissions reflect serious health effects and add to demand for care. They are one part of the total harm caused by polluted air.
cooling_equity_gaps: Some people having much less access than others to shade, safe indoor temperatures and affordable ways to cool down. Poor housing, high electricity costs or unreliable power can contribute. The same hot day can therefore create very different risks for different households.
kelp_forest_collapse: Underwater stands of large seaweed losing so much cover and new growth that they cannot recover normally. These habitats provide food and shelter for many animals. Their loss can change coastal wildlife and fisheries.
trophic_cascade_collapses: A major change in one part of a food chain spreading to other parts. For example, losing a predator can change the animals it eats and then the organisms those animals feed on. The effects depend on the local feeding relationships.
aquifer_recharge_failure: Less water reaching underground stores to replace what has been removed or naturally drained away. Rainfall, land cover and soil conditions affect this refill. A sustained reduction can make wells and other dependent water supplies less reliable.
supply_chain_port_bottlenecks: Goods getting held up because a harbour cannot move ships or cargo through quickly enough. Limits may involve workers, storage, equipment or onward transport. Delays can spread to businesses and consumers far from the port.
coastal_property_insurance_redlines: Insurers declining to renew or offer cover for homes and buildings exposed to hazards near the sea. Repeated flood losses or rising expected costs can contribute. Losing cover can also complicate home loans and property sales.
cloud_albedo_shift: Clouds changing how much sunlight Earth reflects and how much heat it keeps. These effects can oppose one another. Whether the overall change warms or cools the planet depends on the cloud type, height, location and amount.
deep_sea_mining_dust: Clouds of fine seabed material stirred into the water by mineral extraction or waste disposal. The particles can settle on animals and habitats or affect feeding. The area and duration of exposure depend on currents and the operation.
agrochemical_water_sinks: Chemicals used to control pests, or the substances they break down into, remaining in rivers and lakes. They can affect fish, plants and other water-living organisms. Effects depend on the chemical, concentration and length of exposure.
acid_rain_deposition: Acid-forming pollution reaching land and water through rain, snow, gases or particles. It can change soil and water chemistry and affect living things. Local soils, water and pollutant sources determine how much damage occurs.
desertification_frontiers: Dry regions losing healthy soil, vegetation or their ability to support people and wildlife. This can happen through unsuitable land use, drought and other pressures. The result may be less reliable crop or livestock production. It does not simply mean sand dunes spreading.
cfc_saturated_layers: Long-lasting gases in the air that can release chemicals which destroy the protective ozone layer high above Earth. Many contain chlorine or bromine. Their effects can continue long after release because they remain in the atmosphere for years.
arctic_amplification_rates: The northern polar region warming faster than the planet as a whole. Losing reflective snow and ice is one of the processes involved. Faster warming changes frozen ground, sea ice and the conditions faced by northern communities and wildlife.
rainforest_savannization: A moist, densely wooded landscape shifting toward a drier, more open one with fewer trees. Repeated drying, fire and forest loss can contribute. This changes the habitat, water cycle and carbon stored in the landscape.
urban_water_rationing_zones: Limits on when or how much water homes and businesses may use during shortages. Restrictions can help conserve a scarce supply, but interruptions can also create hardship. Saving water successfully should not itself be treated as worsening danger.
asphalt_pavement_heat_absorbers: Dark road and pavement surfaces absorbing sunlight and storing heat. They can release that heat after the sun goes down. Large paved areas can therefore help keep neighbourhoods warm into the night.
heatwave_excess_mortality_rates: Additional deaths attributed to unusually hot conditions, compared with what would have been expected otherwise. Estimating this requires a defined comparison and evidence linking heat to the deaths. It is not simply the total number of deaths during a hot period.
ambient_air_quality_deficit: Outdoor pollution exceeding a stated guideline or legal limit. The comparison must identify the pollutant and the period over which it is measured. Different standards serve different purposes, and exceeding one does not describe every aspect of air quality.
genetic_diversity_bottlenecks: A population shrinking so sharply that it loses some of its inherited variety. With fewer breeding individuals, close relatives may breed more often. This can reduce the population's ability to cope with disease or changing conditions.
palm_oil_canopy_clearance: Forests being permanently cleared to make room for oil-palm plantations. The loss removes habitat and stored carbon. This explanation applies where evidence links the clearing to that crop, rather than assuming every nearby forest loss has the same cause.
fishery_border_dispute_zones: Disagreements between countries or fishing fleets over fish that move across political boundaries. Shifting stocks or catches can strain existing access agreements. Whether a dispute becomes more serious depends on cooperation, enforcement and alternatives.
stratospheric_cooling: Temperatures falling in the layer of air above most clouds and ordinary weather. Changes in heat-trapping gases and ozone can affect this layer differently from the surface. Cooling high above Earth can occur while the surface warms.
inland_waterway_fuel_spills: Oil-based fuel accidentally entering rivers, canals or lakes. Damaged vessels, refuelling accidents or broken tanks can cause releases. Effects depend on the amount spilled, how it spreads and which habitats or water users are exposed.
coral_reef_fragmentation: Connected coral habitat being broken into smaller, separated pieces. Damage can remove shelter and make it harder for organisms to move between suitable areas. The consequences depend on whether growth and recovery can keep pace with the loss.
mountain_pass_avalanches: Masses of snow or ice moving quickly downhill through mountain routes. They can bury roads, railways or power and communication lines. People and services are at risk where these routes cross the path of a slide.
dust_storm_frequency: How often wind lifts enough loose soil or sand to create a major cloud of dust. Dry ground, exposed soil and strong winds influence these events. Airborne particles can reduce visibility and affect health far from their source.
ice_shelf_grounding_line_retreat: The point where a large body of ice leaves the ground and begins floating moving farther inland. Losing contact with the bed can change the resistance to ice flow. In some settings this allows more land ice to move toward the sea.
pollen_allergen_spikes: Short periods with unusually high amounts of allergy-causing plant material in the air. People who are sensitive to it can develop symptoms or worsening asthma. Effects depend on the plant species, weather and individual sensitivity.
estuary_eutrophication: Too many nutrients entering the water where a river meets the sea. This can encourage excessive algae growth, reduce light and use up oxygen during decay. The resulting changes can harm seagrass, fish and other wildlife.
avian_migration_disruptions: Birds travelling between seasonal homes at the wrong time, by altered routes or with fewer suitable stopping places. They may miss food or arrive too late to breed successfully. Repeated problems can reduce survival and population size.
shell_calcification_failures: Animals having difficulty building or maintaining hard shells and skeletons. Water chemistry and other conditions can affect the materials and energy available for growth. Poor growth or survival can also affect animals that depend on them for food or habitat.
arctic_pack_ice_drift: Floating sea ice in the north being moved by winds and ocean currents. It can gather in some places and leave others open. Moving ice can obstruct vessel routes even when the region has less ice overall.
amphibian_chytrid_fungus_spreads: Fungal infection affecting the skin of frogs, salamanders and related animals. Severe infection can disrupt functions they need to survive and cause deaths. The impact varies between species, places and infection levels.
early_warning_coverage_gaps: People not getting a clear alert in time before danger arrives, or not having a way to act on it. Sensors may miss the danger, messages may not reach everyone, or people may lack help to leave. Having an alert system does not mean everyone is protected.
black_carbon_deposition: Dark soot from burning fuel or vegetation settling out of the air onto surfaces. On snow and ice it can reduce the sunlight reflected away. This can increase absorbed heat and speed local melting.
glacial_siltation_streams: Streams carrying large amounts of fine rock particles ground up by moving ice. The particles can cloud the water or settle downstream. Continued buildup may affect river habitats, reservoir capacity and water intakes.
jellyfish_swarm_surges: Changes in how often very large gatherings of jellyfish occur and how much living material they contain. Dense gatherings can interfere with fishing nets and fish farms. Effects depend on the species and where the animals collect.
cryoconite_hole_expansion: Small melt holes on glacier surfaces growing or becoming more numerous around dark dirt and microbes. The dark material absorbs sunlight more readily than clean ice. This can speed melting in the areas where it collects.
bark_beetle_epidemics: Large outbreaks of insects that live and feed beneath tree bark. When attacks overwhelm tree defences, many trees can die. The scale of damage depends on the insects, host trees and surrounding conditions.
old_growth_forest_logging: Cutting trees in forests that have developed over many decades or centuries. Removing large trees and adding access roads can change habitat and stored carbon. Even selective cutting can disturb nearby trees and break up continuous cover.
savannah_tree_cover_decline: Open grassland landscapes losing some of their trees and shrubs. These woody plants provide shade, food and nesting places. Their loss can change the mix of wildlife and how the landscape functions.
particulate_soot_levels: The amount of fine, dark material from burning fuel or vegetation present in the air. It contributes to particle pollution. Where it later settles on snow or ice, it can also darken the surface and increase melting.
pesticide_spray_drift_zones: Pest-control chemicals travelling through the air beyond the place where they were applied. Droplets, dust or vapour can reach nearby people, plants and water. Harm depends on the chemical and the amount and route of exposure.
estuarine_nursery_loss: Sheltered areas where rivers meet the sea becoming less suitable for young fish and other animals. These places provide food and protection while the animals grow. Losing them can reduce the number that survive to join adult populations.
ice_algae_pigmentation: Tiny organisms growing on or near snow and ice adding colour to the surface. Their pigments can change how much sunlight is absorbed. These organisms can also form part of polar food systems, depending on where they grow.
snowpack_dust_soot_coverage: Mineral particles settling on snow and making its surface darker. Darkened snow absorbs more sunlight and can melt earlier. This changes when stored snow-water reaches rivers and exposes the ground beneath.
heavy_metal_bioaccumulation: Metals building up inside living things when they are taken in faster than they are removed. Some can harm growth, reproduction or survival at sufficient doses. Effects depend on the metal, its chemical form and the exposed organism.
glacier_hydrologic_system_floods: Water stored inside, underneath or beside a glacier being released quickly. A sudden release can send a large surge down a valley. Its danger depends on the amount of water and what lies in the flow path.
wetland_peat_fires: Fire burning into the carbon-rich soil of wetlands that have become dry. It can smoulder below the surface and consume material built up over long periods. Burning releases carbon dioxide and smoke, with the amount depending on the area and depth burned.
convective_instability_shift: Changes in how readily warm, moist air can rise and form strong storm clouds. Both the energy available for rising air and the barriers holding it down matter. Storms still require suitable moisture and a way to get started.
ice_cap_decapitation: A small ice-covered region losing its high-elevation area where snow normally builds up. The remaining lower ice may no longer receive enough new snow to replace what melts. Exposed darker ground can also absorb more sunlight.
riparian_zone_erosion: Flowing water wearing away riverbanks and the soil beside streams. This can remove plants and shade and add sediment to the water. Persistent loss changes habitats along the river and can threaten nearby land or structures.
nighttime_heat_retention: Heat stored by buildings, roads and other surfaces being released slowly after sunset. The surrounding area can remain warm when it would normally cool down. Limited vegetation and local air conditions can add to the effect.
nunatak_habitat_shrinkage: Suitable living space becoming smaller or more isolated on rocky mountain areas that rise above surrounding ice. Cold-adapted plants and animals may have fewer places to survive as conditions change. Changes in ice cover alone do not establish how much suitable habitat remains.
biodiversity_corridors_disruption: Living things becoming less able to move between the places they need for food, shelter or breeding. Roads, damaged habitat and other barriers can interrupt these routes. Isolated populations may struggle to recover after losses or reach cooler places as conditions change.
