walker_circulation_shift: Changes in the loop of air moving east and west across the tropical Pacific. Air rises over some warm, rainy areas and sinks over drier areas. Shifts in this loop change winds, ocean conditions and where rainfall tends to occur.
fjord_sedimentation_pulses: Bursts of mud, sand and other particles entering a narrow sea inlet between steep sides. Melting or retreating glaciers can change the supply and timing of this material. It can cloud the water and build up on the bottom.
transformer_heat_failure_risk: The chance that equipment used to change electricity voltage overheats and stops working. Heavy electrical loads and hot surroundings can add to the strain. Failure can interrupt power, and replacement may take time.
freeze_thaw_rock_fracturing: Water inside cracks in rock repeatedly freezing and thawing. Ice formation can widen or weaken existing cracks over time. This can make rock less stable, depending on the water supply, temperatures and structure of the rock.
overstory_tree_mortality: The death of large trees that form a forest's upper leafy layer. Losing them changes shade, habitat and the forest's structure. When many die across an area, the wider forest can struggle to maintain its usual functions.
aerosolized_microplastics: Tiny plastic fibres and fragments floating in the air or settling out of it. Wear, manufacturing and waste handling can release them, and wind can lift previously settled particles. Their presence is different from a demonstrated health effect at a particular dose.
coastal_saltwater_intrusion: Seawater moving inland or upward into places that previously held fresher water. Rivers, soil and underground supplies can be affected. Higher sea levels or heavy pumping of fresh water can contribute, making some supplies less suitable for use.
tundra_shrubification_speeds: Shrubs spreading across northern landscapes previously dominated by lower-growing plants. Warmer growing conditions can favour some species. The pace and effects also depend on snow, soil moisture, grazing and disturbance.
subpolar_gyre_weakening: Changes in the strength and reach of a large rotating system of currents in the northern Atlantic. Winds and exchanges of heat with the air help shape it. The circulation can strengthen or weaken, affecting the movement of water and heat.
shelf_sea_hypoxia: Shallow seas beside continents containing too little dissolved oxygen for many animals. Poor mixing and the breakdown of excess organic material can contribute. Less-tolerant animals may die or move away, changing the local food web.
freshwater_mussel_depletion: Fewer river and lake mussels, fewer kinds of them or fewer places where they live. These shellfish filter water and contribute to habitats on the bottom. Large, lasting losses can therefore affect more than the mussels themselves.
lightning_regime_shifts: Changes in how often lightning occurs, where flashes are concentrated or which seasons they occur in. A flash reaching dry vegetation can start a fire under suitable conditions. Changes in lightning do not by themselves determine how much land burns.
coral_larval_mortality: Young corals failing to survive, settle on a suitable surface or grow into new colonies. Adults then have fewer replacements when they die. Persistent failure can reduce long-term coral cover and the maintenance of reef structure.
riverine_habitat_fragmentation: Rivers being divided into sections that aquatic animals cannot easily travel between. Dams, road crossings, low flows or damaged stretches can create barriers. Animals may lose access to breeding places, food or refuge during harsh conditions.
high_altitude_forest_shrinkage: Wooded areas high in the mountains becoming smaller or less connected. Changes in tree survival and where trees can grow alter shade, food and shelter. Species that depend on these cool, high places may have limited alternatives.
atmospheric_river_intensification: Long bands of moist air carrying more water toward a region, lasting longer or producing heavier rain and snow. When the air rises over mountains or weather fronts, moisture can fall out rapidly. Effects depend on the route, duration and local conditions.
trade_wind_weakening: The usual east-to-west winds near the equator in the Pacific becoming stronger or weaker than their seasonal pattern. These winds influence ocean surface water and tropical rainfall. The sign of the change matters: an unusual reading does not always mean weakening.
blue_carbon_habitat_loss: Coastal habitats such as mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass beds being damaged or removed. These places store carbon in plants and soils. Their loss can release stored carbon and reduce future uptake, which are two different effects.
methane_hydroxyl_sink_loss: The air becoming less able to break down methane and some other gases through chemical reactions. Highly reactive molecules normally help remove them. If that cleaning capacity weakens, the gases can remain in the air longer for the same amount released.
stratospheric_chlorine_sinks: Changes in the amount of ozone high in the atmosphere, including its loss and recovery. This gas absorbs harmful ultraviolet sunlight and helps warm that layer of air. Recovery depends on the chemicals present and atmospheric conditions.
aviation_condensation_trails: Thin lines of ice cloud forming when aircraft exhaust mixes with cold, moist air high above the ground. Some disappear quickly. Others spread and last longer. They change both reflected sunlight and escaping heat, so their effects depend on the conditions.
compound_coastal_flooding: Several sources of high water combining near the sea, such as storm-driven seawater, high tides and heavy river flow. Together they can make drainage harder or flooding deeper. The outcome depends on their timing and the local landscape.
fisheries_range_redistribution: Fish that people catch moving to different places, depths or seasons. Fishing communities may find familiar stocks less accessible, while other places gain access. When fish cross national boundaries, existing sharing agreements may become harder to apply.
coastal_aquifer_degradation: An underground freshwater store near the sea becoming saltier. Water that was suitable for drinking or farming may then need extra treatment or replacement. The causes and effects depend on pumping, seawater movement and the local ground.
food_insecurity: Not having reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food. A household may face shortages, unaffordable prices or difficulty obtaining suitable meals. Producing enough food overall does not guarantee that everyone can get it.
nutrient_pollution: Too much nitrogen or phosphorus entering rivers, lakes or coastal water. These substances help plants grow, but an excess can trigger algae growth and oxygen loss. The damage depends on the receiving water and the amount and timing of the input.
seagrass_meadow_decline: Underwater flowering plants losing area or becoming less healthy. Their beds provide habitat, store carbon and help stabilize the seabed. Less cover can weaken these functions even before a bed disappears completely.
urban_heat_island: A town or city being warmer than a defined nearby non-urban area. Buildings and roads store heat, while limited vegetation provides less shade and cooling. The size of the difference varies by weather, time of day and neighbourhood.
dam_and_diversion_infrastructure: Structures that hold back river water or redirect it for power, farming or other uses. They can change the timing of flows and block movement by aquatic animals. Their effects depend on design, operation and the river involved.
road_stream_crossing_barriers: Places where roads cross waterways and make it difficult for fish or other animals to pass. Pipes, gates or crossing structures may create steep drops, shallow water or fast flows. Whether an animal can pass depends on both the structure and the species.
levee_and_channelization_works: Raised riverbanks or engineered channels used to control where water flows. They can protect some areas while separating rivers from the land they would naturally flood. This changes habitat, water movement and connections along the river.
humanitarian_response_funding_shortfall: Aid operations receiving less money than they need for planned help. Services may have to be delayed, reduced or stopped. The effect depends on which needs remain unmet and whether other support is available.
humanitarian_access_constraints: Obstacles preventing aid workers or supplies from reaching people in a crisis. Conflict, damaged routes, administrative restrictions or attacks can block delivery. Having supplies available elsewhere does not mean they can reach those who need them.
humanitarian_surge_demand: A rapid increase in the number of people needing urgent assistance. Several disasters or conflicts happening together can outpace available staff and supplies. The pressure depends on both the new needs and the ability to expand help.
agricultural_groundwater_withdrawal: Water pumped from underground stores to irrigate crops in a stated place and period. Pumping can reduce reserves if it exceeds replacement. This measure concerns that water use, rather than all the effects of farming.
municipal_groundwater_withdrawal: Water pumped from underground stores for a public supply, such as household and local business use. The amount must be tied to a particular system and period. Its effect depends on how quickly the water is replaced and what else relies on it.
industrial_groundwater_withdrawal: Water pumped from underground stores for factories, mining, power production or other specified business uses. It can compete with other users where supplies are limited. The measure needs to identify which activities and place are included.
agricultural_nitrogen_application: Adding nitrogen-containing products or organic material to farmland to help crops grow. The amount, timing and crop needs influence how much is used by plants. Unused nutrients can be lost to water or air.
anaerobic_manure_lagoon_operation: Keeping animal waste in a pond where it breaks down with little oxygen. This can produce methane, a gas that traps heat. Releases depend on the animals, amount of waste, temperature, storage time and treatment.
cattle_stocking_density: How many cattle, or how much total animal weight, occupy a grazing area over a stated time. Concentrated grazing can increase pressure on plants and soil. Its effects depend on ground conditions and how long the animals remain there.
coal_power_sulfur_emissions: Sulfur-containing pollution released when power stations burn coal. The amount depends on the fuel and pollution-control equipment. It can affect air quality and contribute to acid-forming pollution downwind.
agricultural_soil_compaction: Farmland soil being pressed together so it has less space for air, water and roots. Heavy equipment or livestock can contribute, especially under vulnerable soil conditions. This can limit plant growth and change how rain enters or runs off the ground.
urban_hydrologic_supply_shortfall: A city's available water falling below what its users and operating rules require. Rivers, reservoirs or underground stores may provide too little. The size of the gap depends on demand, stored reserves and other usable supplies.
urban_water_demand_peak: The busiest period of water use across a city or supply network. Treatment plants and pipes must keep up as well as the original water source. A high peak can create shortages even when use averaged over a longer period seems manageable.
urban_distribution_water_loss: Water supplied to a city's network not being recorded as authorized use. Some may escape through leaks. Some may reflect meter errors or unrecorded use. Those causes need to be separated because they do not all represent water physically lost.
urban_source_water_treatment_constraint: Problems with incoming water or treatment equipment limiting how much safe water a city can supply. Salt, pollutants or other quality changes can make available water harder to use. The limit depends on the system's treatment capabilities.
wildfire_smoke_pm25_exposure: People breathing very small particles specifically linked to vegetation fires. The estimate considers where people are and the pollution levels during a stated period. It should distinguish smoke from particles produced by other sources.
wildfire_smoke_exposure_duration: How long people face smoke levels above a stated comparison value, and how often those periods recur. A brief peak and many smoky days describe different patterns. Duration needs to be considered alongside pollution concentration.
surface_water_inflow_deficit: Less water entering a lake, wetland or river than expected for a stated comparison. Low rain, reduced upstream flow or less water running off the land can contribute. Reduced incoming water can lower storage if losses continue.
surface_water_evaporative_loss: Water leaving a lake, wetland or river as vapour into the air. Weather and the exposed water area affect the amount. This loss can reduce available storage, especially when little water flows in to replace it.
surface_water_groundwater_exchange_shift: Changes in water moving between rivers or lakes and underground stores. A waterbody may receive less water from below or lose more through its bed. The direction and amount depend on local water levels and the ground.
surface_water_withdrawal_pressure: Water taken or diverted from a lake, wetland or river compared with what flows in and remains stored. Heavy use can leave less for other users and living systems. The effect depends on timing, returns and available reserves.
coastal_groundwater_withdrawal: Pumping fresh water from underground stores near the sea. Removing too much can lower freshwater levels and allow saltier water to move toward wells. The response depends on local geology, pumping locations and how quickly fresh water is replaced.
coal_power_co2_output: The heat-trapping gas released when coal is burned to generate electricity. The total depends on fuel use and how efficiently stations produce power. This describes releases from the specified power sector, place and period.
gas_power_co2_output: The heat-trapping gas released when natural gas is burned to generate electricity. The amount depends on fuel use and plant efficiency. It does not by itself include every effect of producing and transporting the fuel.
oil_power_co2_output: The heat-trapping gas released when oil-based fuel is burned to generate electricity. Fuel use and plant efficiency affect the amount. The total applies to the power generation covered by the stated data.
coal_industrial_heat_co2: The heat-trapping gas released when factories burn coal to provide heat. Higher fuel use generally creates more releases unless the process changes. These are emissions from supplying heat, which need to be distinguished from chemical reactions in the materials being made.
gas_industrial_heat_co2: The heat-trapping gas released when factories burn natural gas for heat. The total depends on production needs, equipment and fuel use. It is separate from any additional gases released by the industrial process itself.
cement_kiln_fuel_co2: The heat-trapping gas released by fuel used to heat kilns that make the binding material in concrete. These kilns operate at high temperatures. Burning fuel and chemically processing limestone are separate sources and should not be confused.
iron_steel_process_co2: The heat-trapping gas released from fossil fuels and related processes in the metal industries covered by the data. The total depends on what metals and production methods are included. It should not be treated as a measure of every environmental effect of metal-making.
chemical_process_co2: The heat-trapping gas released from fossil fuels and processes in the chemical industry covered by the data. Both energy supply and manufacturing methods matter. The reported amount applies to the specified activities, place and time.
refinery_combustion_co2: The heat-trapping gas released by oil refining and other energy-production activities included in the data. Processing fuels requires energy and can also release carbon through industrial processes. The total depends on which activities are counted.
aviation_jet_fuel_co2: The heat-trapping gas released when civilian aircraft burn fossil fuel. The total depends on flying activity, fuel and efficiency. It does not include all aviation-related warming effects, such as changes caused by persistent ice-cloud trails.
shipping_bunker_fuel_co2: The heat-trapping gas released when vessels burn fossil fuel to travel by water. The total depends on traffic, routes, loads and efficiency. Its coverage follows the types of navigation included in the source data.
passenger_road_fuel_co2: The heat-trapping gas released by fuel burned for passenger journeys on roads. Vehicle efficiency, distance travelled and the number of passengers influence the result. Freight transport and other activities need to be counted separately where the source separates them.
diesel_freight_co2: The heat-trapping gas released when goods vehicles burn diesel. The amount depends on distance, cargo, vehicle efficiency and operating conditions. It measures this fuel-related contribution rather than every impact of moving goods.
rail_diesel_co2: The heat-trapping gas released by fossil fuels used in railway operations covered by the data. Fuel-powered trains release it directly. Electricity generation for electric trains is a separate source unless the accounting explicitly includes it.
residential_gas_heat_co2: The heat-trapping gas released when homes burn natural gas for heating. The amount depends on the buildings, equipment, weather and fuel use. Better insulation or a different heating system can change these releases.
commercial_gas_heat_co2: The heat-trapping gas released when business and public buildings burn natural gas for heating. Building size, use and heating efficiency affect the amount. The figure applies to the buildings and period covered by the data.
oil_building_heat_co2: The heat-trapping gas released when oil-based fuels provide heat in buildings. Fuel use depends on the weather, insulation and heating equipment. This measures the direct fuel-related contribution within the stated coverage.
fossil_power_backup_co2: The heat-trapping gas released by fuel-burning equipment used when the normal electricity supply is unavailable or insufficient. Both the fuel and the time spent running affect the amount. A rarely used generator and a routinely used one have different totals.
waste_incineration_co2: The heat-trapping gas released when fossil-derived material in waste, such as plastics, is burned. The data may cover controlled facilities, open burning or both. This contribution must be distinguished from carbon released by burning plant-based material.
oil_gas_flaring_co2: The heat-trapping gas released by oil and natural-gas industry activities included in the source data. This can include more than burning off unwanted gas. The total applies only to the activities listed in the source.
deforestation_co2_release: The heat-trapping gas released as carbon in cleared trees and soils returns to the air. Burning and decay can both contribute. These releases are distinct from the future carbon uptake lost when the forest is removed.
peatland_drainage_co2: The heat-trapping gas released when drained, carbon-rich wetland soil is exposed to air and decays. Carbon stored over a long time can continue escaping while the material remains exposed. The amount depends on the area and conditions of the soil.
land_use_fire_co2: The heat-trapping gas released when vegetation or soil is burned during land-use activities. The total depends on the area, material and depth burned. This is a specific source of emissions, not a measure of all fires or all later land changes.
construction_material_co2: The heat-trapping gas released while producing the building materials included in the data. Energy use and chemical manufacturing processes can both contribute. The total depends on the materials, production methods and activities counted.
fossil_hydrogen_co2: The heat-trapping gas released when hydrogen is made using fossil fuels. Releases depend on the fuel, production method and any effective carbon capture. Hydrogen's use at its destination does not by itself describe the pollution created during its manufacture.
